assumptions: Read-only is enforced at four independent points — the allow-list, the deny-by-default callback, the block-list, and the absence of any permission bypass — because a preset can reintroduce a tool the allow-list alone would have excluded.
Automatic shell approval inside a sandbox is explicitly switched off here, unlike the task worker, so a sandbox never becomes a reason to permit commands.
The engine runs as a child over the protocol with a session id threaded through, so questions are answered against the graph rather than by reading files alone.
Two identifiers exist and are not interchangeable: the context session used for scoring, and the provider session captured for resuming a later turn.
An absent provider library is a refusal with a reason, not a crash.

sideEffects.description: runs a provider session under a reduced tool set
spawns the engine as a protocol child
reads repository files through the allowed tools

risks: Every refusal path returns a reason rather than throwing, so a caller that checks only for the presence of text cannot tell a refusal from an answer.

Both tool lists are enumerations, so drift costs reach rather than containment: a newly added read tool stays unavailable until it is named on the allow-list, while anything unnamed is refused by the callback and never offered to the session.
A question that runs long holds provider capacity until its own timeout fires, while the channel that asked it keeps waiting.
patterns: Enforcement in the engine rather than in prose: the policy text explains the restriction, the permission callback is what applies it.
Layered denial, so no single misconfigured option can widen the permitted set on its own.
invariants: No permission bypass is ever set on this path.
Shell auto-approval stays off regardless of sandbox state.
The result is an answer shape, never the protocol run result the task workers produce.
An empty reply is reported as a failure rather than returned as a blank answer.
annotation.integrationPoints: Invoked by the question router in mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/ask; the prompt and policy text come from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/ask-prompt; the tool partition and child environment from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/mcp; timeout and sandbox settings from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/claude-config; credentials from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/auth; the engine entry path from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine.
annotation.stateShape: Success returns the answer text and the context session id; every failure returns a refusal carrying a reason.
annotation.dataFlow: question → credential check → prompt built with policy appended → provider session with the read-only tool set and the engine child → streamed assistant text and provider session id → answer text.

envDependencies.CLAUDE_AGENT_VERBOSE: Logs each tool use unless set to 0

annotation.summary: The read-only question path for the local provider. It runs the same turn loop as the local task worker but offers only reading: one file-read tool plus the non-mutating engine tools, and it answers in prose rather than producing a run result. It exists so that selecting the local provider applies to questions too, instead of questions quietly falling through to the other provider's runner.

keyExports.runAsk: Runs the question session and returns the answer text, or a refusal carrying the reason.

assumptions: Read-only is enforced in the dispatcher: the harness executes tools itself here, so a call to anything outside the permitted set returns a refusal to the model instead of running. There is no separate permission layer, because there is no provider runtime to ask.
The engine's tool list is filtered against the read-only allow-list before the model ever sees it, so mutating tools are absent from the offered functions as well as refused at dispatch.

The loop primitives — the completion call, the history compaction, the tool-call normalization and the inline-call recovery — are shared with the task worker rather than reimplemented, so the two stay in step.
A refused tool is answered rather than fatal: the model receives an error result and can continue with a permitted tool.
Reasoning sections are stripped from the visible reply, so they never reach the answer.

sideEffects.description: spawns the engine as a protocol child
sends completion requests to the configured endpoint
reads repository files through the sandboxed reader

risks: When the engine child fails to start the session continues with file reading alone, logging the reason only in verbose mode.

The permitted set enumerates tool names rather than deriving from any property of the tools, so it holds only as long as a permitted name keeps meaning a read. A new engine tool is absent from the offer and refused at dispatch until the list is extended; a permitted tool that gains a mutating mode passes both barriers under its existing name.
A question costs the same per turn as task work despite the smaller tool surface, because the loop, the context and the compaction are shared.
patterns: The harness is the executor, so the refusal lives where the call is made rather than in a policy the provider enforces.
Two barriers with one list: tools are filtered out of the offer and refused at dispatch, so a model that invents a name gets the same answer as one that ignores the offer.
invariants: The permitted set contains no tool that writes, refreshes or annotates.
The result is answer text, never the protocol run result the task workers produce.
Anything outside the permitted set is refused rather than executed.
annotation.integrationPoints: Selected by the question router in mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/ask; the loop primitives and the sandboxed reader come from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/local; the read-only tool list and the child descriptor from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/mcp; the prompt and policy from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/ask-prompt; credentials from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/auth; endpoint settings from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/local-config; accounting through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/usage.
annotation.dataFlow: question → credential check → engine child with the read-only tool list → per-turn compaction then a completion request → dispatch permitted calls, refuse the rest → final prose answer.

envDependencies.LOCAL_VERBOSE: Enables verbose logging for this path

annotation.summary: The prompt for the read-only ask path. The policy tells the agent to orient through the engine's read tools first, to read source when those are not enough, and forbids creating or editing files, refreshing the graph, writing annotations, running any shell command, and emitting a protocol result block. The builder adds the question, the context session id and any attachments.

keyExports.ASK_POLICY: The read-only policy text: engine tools first, no writes, no shell, no protocol result block.
keyExports.buildAskPrompt: Assembles the policy, the question, the context session id and the attachment brief.

assumptions: The answer is plain prose in the question's own language, which is why no result block is requested.
The context session id is included so the agent's engine calls are scored under the same session as the run.
The attachment brief is reused from the worker prompt module rather than duplicated.
risks: The read-only guarantee is prose in the prompt, so it constrains a cooperative agent; the enforced half is the tool list.

Reusing this policy on the implementer path leaves the capability set untouched: that session keeps its write and shell tools and runs with permissions bypassed, while the prose instructs the agent to change nothing. The mismatch is an agent that can act being told not to, not a capability handed over by the prompt.
patterns: The ask path has its own policy separate from the implementer's write policy, so neither can drift into the other by editing shared text.
invariants: The policy forbids file edits, graph refresh, annotation writes and shell commands.
No protocol result block is requested; the answer is the reply itself.
The attachment brief comes from the shared worker prompt module.
annotation.integrationPoints: Reuses the attachment brief from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/prompt; consumed by the provider ask adapters that mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/ask dispatches to.
annotation.dataFlow: question plus the policy, context session id and attachments → buildAskPrompt → provider ask adapter → answer text.

annotation.summary: Shared credential resolver for every harness provider (claude | local). Resolves auth from explicit environment keys only, with no home-login file fallback and no ambient IDE credential probe, so a long-running bot cannot spend against a developer's ambient login. Returns a decision object plus hints and never returns secret values.

keyExports.authBlockedReason: Formats a blocked AgentRunResult reason from a failed resolveAuth outcome.
keyExports.knownProvider: True when the provider id has an entry in the PROVIDERS table (claude | local).
keyExports.resolveAuth: Resolves credentials for a provider, defaulting to LLM_PROVIDER then claude; returns {ok, mode, source} or {ok:false, reason, hints}.

assumptions: Provider keys come from .env under Docker or from the exported environment when running locally.
Explicit env names are read dynamically via spec.explicitEnv.find(name => process.env[name]), so static env detection does not list ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN; both are real.
The local provider treats LOCAL_BASE_URL as the whole credential; LOCAL_API_KEY is optional.

sideEffects.description: reads provider credential and base-url env vars at resolve time

risks: The local provider is deliberately not fail-closed: a reachable LOCAL_BASE_URL is accepted without a key, on the grounds that no remote spend is possible against a local model.

risks.text: Callers must treat a false ok as terminal and surface authBlockedReason; continuing past it runs a provider call with no resolved credential.

patterns: Fail-closed by default: an unknown provider or a missing explicit key returns ok:false with hints rather than falling back.
One PROVIDERS table is the single place a provider's credential contract is declared.
invariants: Credentials come from explicit environment keys only; no home credential file is ever loaded.
resolveAuth never returns a secret value, only which source satisfied the lookup.
An unknown provider returns ok:false with hints naming the supported set.
annotation.integrationPoints: Called at worker startup by mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers, by mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/llm askLLM, and by the planner path in mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/plan.
annotation.dataFlow: provider id or LLM_PROVIDER → PROVIDERS lookup → first non-empty explicit env key (or LOCAL_BASE_URL for local) → {ok, mode, source}, else authBlockedReason for the blocked result.

envDependencies.LLM_PROVIDER: Selects the provider when resolveAuth is called without an explicit id
envDependencies.LOCAL_API_KEY: Optional key for the local provider
envDependencies.LOCAL_BASE_URL: Base URL for the local OpenAI-compatible provider; acts as its credential

annotation.summary: Claude worker adapter shim: re-exports runAgent from lib/claude-agent.mjs and declares provider='claude' so getWorker's dynamic import path stays uniform across providers (LLM_PROVIDER=claude is the default).

keyExports.provider: String 'claude' for logging/routing. The module also re-exports runAgent from lib/claude-agent.mjs (not tracked as a distinct export by the graph, since it is a pass-through re-export).

assumptions: Implementation lives in lib/claude-agent.mjs — this file is adapter re-export only.
The runAgent seam is shared with at least one peer adapter module under lib/workers/.
Auth is resolved inside claude-agent.mjs via resolveAuth; MCP is launched as a stdio server scoped to repoRoot inside the SDK options there.
risks: Changes to lib/claude-agent.mjs affect all claude worker paths without touching this file.
patterns: Thin adapter module — keeps graph run_worker import path uniform per provider.
invariants: The provider const must stay 'claude' for routing to work.
annotation.integrationPoints: mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/claude-agent (runAgent, auth, MCP stdio wiring); consumed by lib/workers/index.mjs getWorker.
annotation.dataFlow: getWorker('claude') -> imports claude.mjs -> re-exported runAgent from claude-agent.mjs.

annotation.summary: Shared Claude provider configuration for task and /ask workers: resolves the worker timeout (a caller-selected primary env, then WORKER_TIMEOUT_MS, then a 600000ms fallback) and builds the Claude Agent SDK sandbox option. The sandbox is FAIL-CLOSED (failIfUnavailable: true) so an unavailable OS sandbox errors rather than silently running unsandboxed with bypassPermissions on.

keyExports.claudeSandbox: Returns SDK sandbox options unless CLAUDE_SANDBOX is explicitly off; callers choose autoAllowBashIfSandboxed.
keyExports.claudeTimeoutMs: Reads a primary timeout env, then WORKER_TIMEOUT_MS, then fallbackMs.

assumptions: Task worker passes primaryEnv CLAUDE_AGENT_TIMEOUT_MS by default; the ask worker passes ASK_TIMEOUT_MS — both read dynamically via process.env[primaryEnv], not statically.
autoAllowBashIfSandboxed is caller-controlled because task and ask have different execution policies.

sideEffects.description: Reads CLAUDE_SANDBOX, WORKER_TIMEOUT_MS, and caller-selected timeout env from process.env

risks: Changing default sandbox options affects both lib/claude-agent.mjs and lib/workers/ask-claude.mjs.
autoAllowBashIfSandboxed is intentionally caller-controlled because task and ask have different execution policies.
invariants: CLAUDE_SANDBOX in {0,false,off,none} (case-insensitive) returns undefined (no sandbox options); otherwise sandboxing is enabled.
claudeSandbox always sets failIfUnavailable: true when enabled — fail closed, not degrade-to-unsandboxed.
annotation.integrationPoints: Imported by lib/claude-agent.mjs and lib/workers/ask-claude.mjs.
annotation.dataFlow: Claude task/ask adapter -> claudeTimeoutMs for SDK timeout; adapter -> claudeSandbox({ autoAllowBashIfSandboxed }) -> query options.

envDependencies.CLAUDE_SANDBOX: Set to 0/false/off/none to opt out of the Claude SDK sandbox.
envDependencies.WORKER_TIMEOUT_MS: Shared fallback worker timeout when the primary env is unset.

annotation.summary: The worker for the vendor-neutral local provider. There is no provider SDK: it spawns the engine as an MCP child and speaks the protocol directly, then runs its own multi-turn loop against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, offering file read, patch apply and shell alongside the engine tools. Because a bare endpoint enforces nothing, this module owns the sandbox, the secret scrubbing, the turn budget and the history compaction itself.

keyExports.resolveInSandbox: Resolves a path against the workspace root and rejects it when it escapes — by parent traversal or through a symlink. An absolute path is accepted when it lands inside the root. Writes additionally refuse anything under the repository's own version-control directory.

assumptions: Every bound the loop respects is enforced here, since the endpoint offers no turn, context or spend limits of its own.
The characters-to-tokens ratio is calibrated from reported usage as the run proceeds, so compaction sizing improves rather than relying on a fixed estimate.
Inline tool-call parsing exists because a model without native tool calling still emits calls as prose; it is recovery, not the primary path.

Containment is judged on where a path lands, not on how it was written: an absolute path inside the workspace is accepted deliberately, because weak models routinely echo the workspace root back into their own arguments. A real escape is still caught by the containment check that follows.
The symlink check is unconditional and applies to reads as well as writes: the deepest existing ancestor is resolved through links and re-checked for containment.
The only write-specific restriction is the refusal to write inside the repository's version-control directory.

sideEffects.description: spawns the engine MCP child and shell actions
sends completion requests to the configured endpoint
reads files through the sandbox resolver
applies patches inside the workspace

risks: Inline tool-call recovery is heuristic, so a model that formats a call unusually has it read as prose and the turn produces no action.
A context budget set above the model's real window cannot be saved by compaction; the request overflows and the run ends blocked with a hint rather than silently truncated.

Containment is the boundary between a model-supplied path and the wider filesystem, and it is decided after resolution rather than by rejecting path shapes — so the correctness of the resolution and the symlink re-check is what holds the line, not any syntactic filter.
Secret scrubbing matches variable names against a fixed pattern, so a credential stored under a name that does not match it reaches a shell action unredacted.
patterns: No vendor SDK: the engine is a protocol child and the endpoint is plain HTTP, which is what makes the provider swappable.
Compaction evicts whole tool rounds rather than trimming messages, so the history stays coherent as it shrinks.
invariants: No Git repository discovery ever runs inside an attached workspace from the patch path.
A malformed target environment fails toward the no-repository patch path, which is the safe choice in every mode.
A path that resolves outside the workspace is rejected rather than clamped, whether it escaped by traversal or through a symlink.
Secret-looking environment variables are removed before any shell action, matched by name pattern.
annotation.integrationPoints: Dispatched through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers; credentials from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/auth, settings from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/local-config, the engine descriptor from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/mcp, and result normalization shared with mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/claude-agent.
annotation.dataFlow: assignment → auth → engine MCP child → per-turn compaction then a completion request → tool calls dispatched to the engine or the sandbox → results appended → final text synthesized into the protocol result.

annotation.summary: Configuration for the vendor-neutral local provider. Separates client wiring, an OpenAI-compatible base URL with an optional key, from per-run options: the model for the role, sampling, and the turn, context and output budgets that bound a loop with no provider-side limits. The premise is that the model is configuration, so switching models is an environment change rather than a code change.

keyExports.localApiKey: The optional key; the base URL is what actually gates access.
keyExports.localBaseUrl: The endpoint, normalized; its presence is the credential for this provider.
keyExports.localClientOptions: The client wiring assembled from base URL and key.
keyExports.localContextTokens: Soft prompt-token budget the loop compacts toward; zero disables compaction.
keyExports.localMaxWriteBytes: Cap on a single write the loop may perform.
keyExports.localRunOptions: Per-run options: resolved model for the role, sampling, turn budget and the engine MCP descriptor.
keyExports.localShellTimeoutMs: Timeout for a shell action inside the loop.
keyExports.localTemperature: Sampling temperature when set to a finite value.
keyExports.stripReasoning: Removes leaked reasoning blocks from a model reply.

assumptions: A bare chat endpoint offers no server-side turn, context or spend limits, so every bound here is enforced by the harness rather than by the provider.
The base URL doubles as the credential, which is why the local provider is deliberately not fail-closed on a missing key.
Reasoning blocks are stripped defensively because some local models emit them inline rather than in a separate channel.

sideEffects.description: reads the local provider settings from the environment at call time

risks: A misconfigured base URL surfaces as an opaque network failure rather than a configuration error, since nothing validates the endpoint before the first call.

risks.text: Every budget defaults to a value rather than to unlimited, so a local run silently stops at a bound instead of running away; a caller reading a truncated result must check which bound it hit.

patterns: Client wiring and per-run options are separated, so a model or role change does not touch the transport configuration.
annotation.integrationPoints: Consumed by the local worker and the local ask adapter; the model for a role comes from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/model-role and the engine MCP descriptor from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/mcp.
annotation.dataFlow: environment -> the individual getters -> client options and per-run options -> the local completion loop.

envDependencies.LOCAL_BASE_URL: OpenAI-compatible endpoint; its presence is the credential
envDependencies.LOCAL_CONTEXT_TOKENS: Soft prompt-token budget the loop compacts to; 0 disables compaction
envDependencies.LOCAL_SHELL_TIMEOUT_MS: Timeout for a shell action inside the loop

annotation.summary: Shared wiring for the repovine MCP server a worker or ask agent talks to. Builds the stdio spawn descriptor and the environment block that pins the engine to the run's workspace and context session, and declares the three tool lists that separate a read-only ask agent from a write-capable implementer.

keyExports.REPOVINE_ASK_MCP_TOOLS: Read-only tool list for the ask path: navigation, dependency and config views, build and annotation status, validation.
keyExports.REPOVINE_WORKER_MCP_TOOLS: The implementer list: the read-only set plus refresh, annotation writes and the merge tools.
keyExports.REPOVINE_WRITE_MCP_TOOLS: The mutating tools, named explicitly so the read-only path can deny them rather than rely on omission.
keyExports.buildRepovineMcpStdio: The stdio MCP server descriptor launching the engine CLI with that environment.
keyExports.repovineMcpEnv: The environment block pinning the engine workspace root and, when present, the context session id.

assumptions: The environment block is built fresh rather than merged over the parent, so only what the caller passes reaches the MCP child. Every worker and ask path opts into inheriting the process environment, because the agent SDK replaces the child environment rather than extending it and the local adapter spawns the child directly.
The context session id is set only when one is supplied, so a session-less call does not create a stray session.
The engine entrypoint path comes from the shared CLI wrapper rather than being resolved here.

sideEffects.description: the descriptor it returns causes an engine MCP subprocess to be spawned per worker session

risks: A wrong engine entrypoint path breaks every provider's MCP wiring at once, since all of them build their descriptor here.

Both read-only paths close on the ask list alone: a tool absent from it never runs. The write list names the mutating tools for a second, redundant block, so keeping it in sync is not what makes the path read-only.
patterns: The mutating tools are enumerated as their own list rather than left implicit, so the read-only path denies by name instead of by absence.
invariants: The ask list contains no annotation write and no refresh.
The worker list is the ask list extended, so a tool available to the read-only path is never withheld from an implementer.
annotation.integrationPoints: Consumed by the provider worker and ask adapters when they construct their MCP configuration; the engine entrypoint path comes from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine.
annotation.dataFlow: workspace root and context session id -> environment block -> stdio descriptor -> provider adapter spawns the engine MCP with the tool list its role allows.

annotation.summary: MCP tool-call metrics for a harness run. Aggregates the per-call echoes a sub-agent produced into counts by tool and run totals, sourcing them from the compliance report's contextQuality block when present and falling back to the on-disk context-session file, then rolls sub-agent rows into the run-level MCP ledger and formats a one-line summary for the channel. Reviewed against current source: 9-export surface unchanged from the prior note.

keyExports.buildRunMcp: Rolls sub-agent rows into a run total plus a per-sub-agent breakdown.
keyExports.byToolFromEchoes: Counts MCP calls grouped by tool name from a list of echoes.
keyExports.formatMcpMetrics: One-line summary listing the top tools by call count.
keyExports.mcpMetricsFromContextQuality: Extracts metrics from a compliance report's contextQuality block.
keyExports.mcpMetricsFromEchoes: Builds the metrics record (totals plus by-tool counts) from echoes.
keyExports.mcpMetricsFromSessionFile: Reads the cached context-session file and derives metrics from it.
keyExports.resolveMcpMetrics: Prefers the compliance report, falling back to the session file.
keyExports.snapshotMcpSession: Pre-compliance metrics snapshot taken straight from the session store.
keyExports.totalMcpMetrics: Sums compatible metric records into one total.

assumptions: Metrics from the compliance report are preferred over reading the session file, which is the fallback when the report is absent.
Session ids are validated against a pattern before any filesystem access, so a supplied id cannot walk outside the session cache.
A snapshot may be taken before compliance runs, which is why the session-file path exists at all.

sideEffects.description: reads the cached context-session JSON under the engine cache directory when no compliance report is available

risks: A missing or unreadable session file yields no metrics rather than an error, so an empty MCP ledger can mean either no tool calls or an unavailable source.

risks.text: Callers must treat absent metrics as unknown rather than zero when attributing MCP usage; the two are not distinguished in the rolled-up ledger.

patterns: Two sources, one shape: both the compliance report and the session file are normalized into the same metrics record before aggregation.
invariants: Session ids are pattern-validated before the session cache is read.
The compliance report takes precedence over the session file when both are available.
annotation.integrationPoints: Fed by the context-session data the repovine MCP server records; rolled up alongside token accounting in mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/usage and written into the run ledger by mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/multi for the HTTP, Telegram and CLI status surfaces.
annotation.dataFlow: sub-agent MCP calls → contextQuality echoes or cached session file → resolveMcpMetrics → per-sub-agent rows → buildRunMcp → run MCP ledger → formatMcpMetrics for the reply.

annotation.summary: Composes the prompt a provider worker receives. Selects the policy text from the assignment's context phase, resolves the role brief from the engine with a built-in fallback, and appends the honesty rules and the result-shape contract. The policy instructs an explore run to stay read-only and an annotate run to touch annotations only.

keyExports.ANNOTATION_ONLY_POLICY: The annotate policy, permitting annotation writes and nothing else.
keyExports.WRITE_ONLY_POLICY: The default implementer policy: edit files, do not execute.
keyExports.attachmentsBrief: Renders the task's attachments into a prompt section.
keyExports.buildWorkerPrompt: Assembles the final prompt from policy, brief, task and assignment fields.
keyExports.policyForAssignment: Selects the policy from the assignment's context phase.
keyExports.resolveHarnessBrief: Fetches the role brief from the engine, falling back when it is unavailable.

assumptions: The context phase on the assignment is the single input that decides the policy, so the phase is what actually constrains the run rather than the role name.
The brief comes from the engine so it stays in sync with the projected agent assets; the built-in fallback exists only for an engine too old to provide one.
The contract is provider-agnostic: the same honesty rules and policy text go to every worker adapter.

sideEffects.description: shells out to the engine CLI to fetch the role brief
logs when the brief could not be resolved and the fallback was used

risks: A wrong context phase on the assignment hands a run the wrong policy, so an exploration or annotation run is instructed as though it were an implementation.
The fallback brief is materially weaker than the engine-provided one, so an engine version mismatch silently degrades the contract.

risks.text: Explore- and annotate-phase results have filesChanged, graphNodesTouched and annotationsWritten forced empty, so a sub-agent that edits source in a read-only phase reports nothing changed and the run's compliance gates see a clean read-only result.

patterns: Policy is data selected by phase rather than branching in each adapter, so a new provider inherits the same constraints.
invariants: Phase selects the policy text prepended to the prompt; both adapters expose the same file-write, patch, shell and write_annotation tools in every phase.
The prompt always carries the run id, scope, acceptance criteria and requested checks from the assignment.
annotation.integrationPoints: Fetches the brief through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine and logs through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/log; the assembled prompt is consumed by the provider worker adapters, and the attachment renderer is reused by the planner.
annotation.dataFlow: assignment and task -> policy selected by phase plus the resolved role brief and attachments -> buildWorkerPrompt -> provider adapter -> structured run result.

annotation.summary: Token and cost accounting for harness runs. Normalizes each provider's raw usage surface into one additive record (Claude result messages, local OpenAI-compatible usage objects), sums compatible records, and rolls a run's per-sub-agent rows into the run-level ledger written to .harness/<run>.run.usage.json.

keyExports.buildRunUsage: Aggregates rows {subAgent, role, fresh, ok, usage} into run totals plus a per-sub-agent breakdown.
keyExports.claudeModelId: Picks the dominant model id from a Claude result message by usage weight.
keyExports.claudeUsage: Extracts normalized usage and cost from a Claude SDK result message.
keyExports.emptyUsage: Zeroed usage record for a provider/model pair.
keyExports.localUsage: Normalizes a local OpenAI-compatible usage object against a known model id.
keyExports.totalUsage: Sums compatible usage records and recomputes the cache hit ratio.

assumptions: Callers pass the raw SDK usage surface captured by the provider adapter.
Accounting is additive: inputTokens is the uncached remainder, so total prompt = inputTokens + cacheReadTokens + cacheCreationTokens.
Fresh sub-agent rows are the cold-cache measurements; resumed rows measure cache-heavy continuation cost.

risks.text: Callers must key attribution rows by subAgent; the former leaf key is no longer accepted as a usage identity alias and silently loses attribution.

risks: Mixing records from different providers yields provider 'mixed', which makes per-provider cost attribution unrecoverable downstream.
invariants: Missing numeric fields stay null rather than 0, so absent data is distinguishable from zero usage.

totalUsage returns null for an empty or all-null list. Across differing providers it labels the roll-up 'mixed' and carries the last row's model id as the total's model, so the roll-up header alone does not identify what produced the numbers.
buildRunUsage emits no legacy leaves or leafCount fields in the user-facing ledger.
annotation.integrationPoints: Provider workers populate opts.capture.usage; mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/sub-agent rolls per-attempt usage and mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/multi writes the run ledger consumed by mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/mcp-telemetry.
annotation.dataFlow: worker usage capture → sub-agent totalUsage → multi buildRunUsage → .harness/<run>.run.usage.json + telemetry.run_usage → HTTP/Telegram/CLI metrics.

annotation.summary: Host mount adapter for the attach launcher: enumerates the host mount table (/proc/self/mountinfo) and proves the filesystem type under every bind source before attach mode is allowed to proceed. Fail-closed throughout — any condition where mounts cannot be conclusively enumerated or classified throws PreflightError rather than returning an empty/partial result.

keyExports.PreflightError: Error subclass thrown for every attach preflight failure; carries a `check` field (e.g. 'mount-table', 'fs-type').
keyExports.assertProvableFsType: Throws PreflightError('fs-type') if any path in `paths` sits on an unprovable filesystem type (9p, drvfs, virtiofs, nfs/nfs4, cifs, smb3, smbfs, sshfs, any fuse.*, overlay); on WSL additionally requires ext4.
keyExports.isWslHost: Detects WSL via WSL_DISTRO_NAME env var or /microsoft/i match in /proc/version text; a read failure returns false (fails open to non-WSL, safe because unprovable fs-types are denied on every host regardless).
keyExports.mountForPath: Finds the mount p lives on via longest-mountPoint-prefix match; on equal-length ties the LATER table entry wins (mountinfo lists mounts in mount order, so the last line at a point is the active overmount). Throws if no mount contains p.
keyExports.parseMountinfo: Parses /proc/self/mountinfo text into [{ mountPoint, fsType }], decoding octal escapes in mount points. Any line that fails to parse poisons the whole table (throws) rather than being skipped, since skipping could hide the mount that matters.
keyExports.pathContains: Case-sensitive, byte-exact containment check via path.relative — true when p equals parent or lives under it. No filesystem access; both paths must already be canonical (realpath).
keyExports.readHostMountTable: Reads mountinfoText (test seam) or the file at path (default /proc/self/mountinfo) and returns { mounts }. Throws PreflightError on unreadable file, empty text, or zero parsed mounts.

sideEffects.description: fs.readFileSync of /proc/self/mountinfo and /proc/version (both overridable via params for tests)

risks: Filesystem-type provability is an allowlist-by-exclusion (UNPROVABLE_FS_TYPES + fuse.* prefix); a new projection/network filesystem type not in that set would silently pass assertProvableFsType.

risks.text: pathContains and mountForPath require both parent/mount-point and target paths to already be canonicalized (realpath) by the caller; passing unresolved or symlinked paths defeats the containment guarantee.

annotation.summary: Host-side trust boundary for attach mode. The preflight subcommand validates the target and creates nothing; the run subcommand re-runs that full fail-closed preflight, then lays out the state directory with restrictive permissions, prepares the disposable baseline repository, and only then starts the containers. The baseline is committed from the source's tracked file set rather than from the physical working tree.

keyExports.launchFilePath: Path of the launch descriptor for an environment.
keyExports.mountsBelow: Mount points strictly below the given roots.
keyExports.parseWorktreeList: Parses `git worktree list --porcelain` output into worktree entries.
keyExports.preflight: The full validation sequence; pure checking, raising a check-named error on failure.
keyExports.prepareLaunch: Creates the launch descriptor for a checkout at a chosen base revision.
keyExports.resolveLaunchEnv: Reads and validates the launch descriptor, resolving the invoking user and group.
keyExports.restartLaunch: Preflight, then restart the containers without recreating state.
keyExports.runLaunch: Preflight, then state creation and baseline preparation, then compose through an injectable exec seam.
keyExports.walkWorktree: lstat walk that rejects sockets, FIFOs, device nodes and hardlinked files.

assumptions: The compose invocation is injected, so the whole launch path is testable without Docker.
The invoking user and group are resolved on the host and carried into the container so bind-mounted files keep their ownership.
The baseline repository lives in launch state, which is why preparing it never touches the source repository's history.

PreflightError, parseMountinfo and pathContains are re-exported pass-throughs from ./attach-host-adapter.mjs (the module boundary callers/tests import from) rather than symbols defined here, so they are not this module's own graph-recognized exports.

sideEffects.description: runs git probes on the host and starts containers through the injected compose seam
the run path creates the control and runtime directories, the git guard file, and the launch descriptor under the attach state directory
reads the launch descriptor, the mount table and the worktree while validating

risks: Invoking compose directly with hand-set environment bypasses this preflight entirely; that override is documented as unsupported rather than prevented.
Validation covers what the host can observe at launch time, so a target mutated after preflight and before container start is not re-checked.
patterns: Fail closed and in order: nothing is created and no container starts until every check has passed.
Check-named failures let the operator see which specific guarantee was violated rather than a generic error.
invariants: No Docker invocation happens before every check passes, and preflight on its own creates nothing.
The baseline is the source's tracked file set, not the physical working tree: tracked-but-ignored files are excluded.
The launcher never removes worktrees, state, branches or refs, and never commits into the source repository.

The operator record carrying host paths is never mounted. The guard file beside it is bind-mounted read-only as the container's .git, and the container refuses to run unless those bytes match the pointer constant.
annotation.integrationPoints: Writes the guard file whose expected content is defined by mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/attach-guard and reads the launch environment through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/env-file. What it prepares on the host is what the in-container validation later asserts.
annotation.dataFlow: operator command → resolveLaunchEnv → preflight checks over the worktree, mounts and git state → state layout and baseline repository → compose start → the container validates the same target from the inside.

annotation.summary: Host-neutral `docker compose` front end for the harness demo's sandbox profiles (cli/http/tg-bot/down). Builds structured argv (no shell) so literal `*` in `down` and paths with spaces reach compose un-globbed on Linux/macOS/Windows. Invoked via `node scripts/compose.mjs <cli|http|tg-bot|down> [args]`; attach mode has its own separate entrypoint (scripts/attach-launcher.mjs) — this wrapper only touches attach services via `down`.

keyExports.normalizeHostPaths: Resolves HARNESS_WORKSPACE_DIR / HARNESS_AGENTS_HOST_DIR relative overrides against the demo root (DEMO_ROOT); absolute values pass through unchanged.
keyExports.planCompose: Builds the compose invocation plan { args, env, cwd, workspaceDir } for a subcommand (cli/http/tg-bot/down); throws on an unknown subcommand. `down` merges DUMMY_ATTACH_ENV so the attach overlay's required ${VAR:?} binds interpolate without creating any directory.
keyExports.runCompose: Pre-creates the workspace host dir (fs.mkdirSync recursive) as the invoking user when the plan calls for it, then invokes the injectable `exec` (defaults to spawnSync('docker', ...)). The exec seam keeps tests from starting Docker.
keyExports.workspaceHostDir: Absolute host path of the sandbox workspace dir, defaulting to <DEMO_ROOT>/.workspace.

assumptions: Docker CLI is on PATH; runCompose's default exec shells out to the literal command 'docker'.

sideEffects.description: fs.mkdirSync(workspaceDir, { recursive: true }) before running compose
spawnSync('docker', args, { stdio: 'inherit' }) via the default exec

annotation.integrationPoints: infra:docker-compose:examples/agent-harness-demo/compose.attach.yaml — the `down` subcommand stacks compose.yaml + compose.attach.yaml with dummy attach env vars so it can also remove attach containers.

annotation.summary: The command-line entry: run one goal through the same compiled graph the other channels use, print the reply, and exit with a code that reflects whether the work actually passed. Intended for continuous integration and local debugging, where there is no conversation to hold state.

keyExports.default: Top-level script — no exports; runs buildGraph + invokeGraph with cli thread id.

assumptions: The project environment file is read before the process environment is consulted, so credentials configured for the containers are picked up.

Preflight runs in dependency order rather than cost order: the goal argument, then the target, then whether the engine command line is reachable, then the provider name. The target step seeds or wipes the sandbox and the engine step spawns the CLI, so both expensive steps precede the free provider comparison.
The protocol gates run against the built engine command line, so a missing build is reported as such rather than surfacing later as a failed run.
Only real workers run: without credentials the worker reports blocked and the graph still validates and reports it, so there is no silent substitution.
Multiple roles or a review request switch the run to the multi-agent path, where each sub-agent is its own validated assignment and its own compliance judgement.
The goal flag is the outward name and the older task flag remains an alias, since the wire keeps the original key.

sideEffects.description: reads the project environment file
runs provider sessions through the graph
writes run artifacts under the workspace
exits with a status reflecting the outcome

risks: The exit code is the only machine-readable outcome, so a caller that ignores it treats a blocked run — missing credentials, for instance — as a completed one.
Success requires both completion and compliance, and in the multi-agent path every sub-agent must clear both; one sub-agent short of that fails the run.
Credentials are only exercised when a worker starts, so a misconfigured provider passes every preflight and fails part way into a run.
The exit status does not identify which preflight check failed: a missing goal, an unusable target and an unknown provider all exit 2, and only an unreachable engine exits 1.
patterns: Same graph, different trigger: the entry differs from the service and chat entries only in how a goal arrives and how the outcome is reported.
Preflight before spend: everything checkable without a provider is checked first.
invariants: A zero exit means the run completed and passed compliance.
A blocked run is a non-zero outcome.
No mock worker exists on this path.
annotation.integrationPoints: The graph comes from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/workflow; the target and its preparation from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/target-repo; the role catalog from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/roles-catalog; provider selection from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers; the engine command line and its protocol version from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine; the environment file loader from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/env-file. Run artifacts and accounting land through mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/telemetry and mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers/usage.
annotation.dataFlow: arguments and environment file → target, provider and engine preflight → compiled graph → one invocation on a per-run thread → printed reply and touched graph nodes → exit status.

envDependencies.HARNESS_GREENFIELD_PARALLEL: Set to 0 to disable parallel worktree fan-out on a greenfield run
envDependencies.LLM_PROVIDER: Which worker provider to use: claude or local

annotation.summary: The service entry: compile the graph once and start the HTTP channel on it. Most of the code is preflight and one deliberate safety decision — where the server is allowed to listen, and whether it may do so without a token.

keyExports.default: Top-level script — no exports; runs buildGraph + startHttp.

assumptions: The bind address depends on where the process runs. Inside a container it listens on every interface, because the exposure is already restricted where the port is published; on a host it defaults to loopback.
Binding a routable address without a token is refused outright rather than warned about, so a bare local launch cannot put the goal, question and reset endpoints on the network.
Running on loopback without a token is allowed but logged plainly, since the endpoints are open to anything that can reach the port.
The project environment file is read before the process environment, so container-configured credentials apply while an inline variable still wins.
Preflight order puts the provider check and the engine reachability check ahead of binding, so a misconfigured launch fails before it accepts a request.
Only real workers run: without credentials the worker reports blocked and the graph still validates and reports it in the response.

sideEffects.description: reads the project environment file
listens on the configured address and port
exits non-zero when startup fails; one code covers several unrelated causes, so only the logged line identifies which check failed

risks: The container path binds every interface unconditionally, so the safety of that deployment rests entirely on how the port is published; publishing it broadly reintroduces exactly what the host path refuses to do.
Loopback without a token is a supported configuration, so anything else on the same host — another user, another container sharing the namespace — can run agents and trigger a reset.
A port already in use ends startup; there is no fallback scan, so a supervisor that restarts on failure loops rather than recovering.
Credentials are exercised only when a worker starts, so the server accepts requests and reports blocked runs rather than refusing to start.
patterns: Refuse rather than warn where the consequence is network exposure, and warn rather than refuse where it is not.
The graph is compiled once at startup and shared by every request, so per-request cost is the run itself.
invariants: A routable bind without a token never happens on the host path.
The engine command line is verified reachable before the server accepts anything.
The compiled graph is built exactly once.
annotation.integrationPoints: The channel itself is mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/channels/http-adapter; the graph comes from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/workflow; target resolution and preparation from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/target-repo; the role catalog from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/roles-catalog; provider selection from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers; engine reachability from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine; the environment file loader from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/env-file.
annotation.dataFlow: environment file and variables → provider, target and engine preflight → bind address decided and refused if unsafe → graph compiled → channel started.

envDependencies.HARNESS_HTTP_BIND: Host bind address, defaulting to loopback
envDependencies.HARNESS_HTTP_TOKEN: Bearer token; without it the endpoints are open
envDependencies.REPOVINE_IN_DOCKER: Marks the containerized path, where every interface is bound

annotation.summary: The chat entry: compile the graph once and start the messaging channel on it. Thin by design — all orchestration lives in the graph and the channel is transport and access control — so what this file contributes is the refusal to start in any configuration that would accept the wrong people.

keyExports.default: Top-level script — no exports; runs buildGraph + startTelegram.

assumptions: A bot of this kind is publicly messageable, so the allowlist is fail-closed: it is empty unless supplied, no owner identity is compiled in, and an empty list ends startup rather than running a bot that would ignore everyone.
That design means a stray launch can never accidentally accept anyone, which is the reason the empty case is an error rather than a permissive default.
Two environment files are read in order — the project one, then an optional one in the home directory — so a container deployment and a local run configure the same variables from different places.
The engine command line is verified before polling starts, and the failure message distinguishes an absent binary from one that failed to answer, since the two need different fixes.
Only real workers run; there is no mock path on this entry.

sideEffects.description: reads the project and home environment files
polls the messaging API and sends replies through the channel
exits non-zero on any failed precondition, under two codes that group the failures rather than name one

risks: Everyone outside the allowlist is dropped silently, so a wrong identity in the list is indistinguishable from a bot that is not running.

The bot token grants full control of the bot, and it is read from a file on disk; the hardened deployment keeps it out of this process entirely by routing through a proxy that injects it, but a direct launch holds it in the environment.
Provider credentials are not checked at startup, so the bot polls and accepts commands whose runs then report blocked.
patterns: Fail closed on identity, fail early on reachability: who may talk to it is settled before the process starts, and what it depends on is verified before it accepts anything.
The entry stays thin so the three channels share one orchestrator rather than three variations of it.
invariants: An empty allowlist prevents startup.
No identity is hardcoded anywhere in the launch path.
Polling begins only after the engine command line answers.
annotation.integrationPoints: The channel is mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/channels/telegram-adapter; the graph comes from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/graph/workflow; target resolution and preparation from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/target-repo; the role catalog from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/roles-catalog; provider selection from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/workers; engine reachability from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/repovine; the environment file loader from mod:repovine-agent-harness-demo/lib/env-file.
annotation.dataFlow: environment files → token and allowlist checks → provider, target and engine preflight → graph compiled → channel polling started.

envDependencies.TELEGRAM_ALLOWED_IDS: Comma-separated sender allowlist; empty means nobody and startup fails
envDependencies.TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN: Bot credential; startup fails without it

annotation.summary: A development script that runs both build stages against the current repository, prints what they produced, and writes the snapshot and the graph to the cache directory. Despite its name it is not the package surface: nothing imports it, it exports nothing, and it exists to exercise the pipeline without the server around it.
assumptions: Both stages are called directly, so the pipeline can be exercised without the server runtime, the annotation store or any tool wiring in the way.
The printed summary is the point: import resolution counts, node and edge totals by type and kind, and a couple of sample queries that prove the graph is navigable.
Both dumps land in the cache directory, which is not tracked, so running it leaves the working tree clean.
It runs at module top level and is invoked directly rather than imported.

sideEffects.description: scans the whole repository through the first stage
writes the snapshot and graph dumps into the cache directory
prints the stage summaries and sample query output

risks.text: The file name suggests a package entry point, but the published surface is the command-line and server entries; a consumer wiring against this path gets a script that runs a full scan and prints to standard output on import.

risks: It scans the entire repository unconditionally, so on a large tree it is a full cold build rather than a quick check.
The sample queries pick a module by name matching, so on a repository without a matching path those sections print nothing and the run still looks successful.
patterns: The smallest end-to-end path through the pipeline: two stage calls and a print, with nothing in between to hide a failure.
annotation.flowDescription: Dev smoke path: resolve repoRoot → collectRepositoryFactsAsync → composeRepositoryGraph → print import resolution stats and graphStats.
invariants: It starts no server and writes no annotations.
It exports nothing.
Its output goes to the cache directory and standard output only.
annotation.integrationPoints: Calls the two stages directly through mod:repovine/src/stage1 and mod:repovine/src/stage2, queries the result through mod:repovine/src/graph, and resolves the repository and cache locations through mod:repovine/src/paths. It is not part of the server entry path.
annotation.stateShape: None; it holds the snapshot and graph only for the length of the run.
annotation.dataFlow: repository root → first stage snapshot → second stage graph → printed statistics and sample queries → snapshot and graph dumps written to the cache directory.

annotation.summary: The built-in agent manifests: one definition per repovine role, each declaring the tools that role is allowed, the result fields it must return, the client surfaces it projects into, and per-client model hints. The definition list is the source of truth that the MCP manifest tool serves and that the onboarding path renders into client agent files.

keyExports.ANNOTATION_WRITER_DEF: The annotation specialist, whose tool set covers the annotate phase.
keyExports.BUILTIN_AGENT_DEFS: The ordered definitions, the source of truth for the specialist agents.
keyExports.BUILTIN_MANIFESTS: The manifests projected out of those definitions.
keyExports.BuiltinAgentDef: One definition: a manifest plus optional model hints.
keyExports.ManifestModelHints: Per-client model hints for an agent, covering the supported client surfaces.
keyExports.getManifestByRole: The canonical manifest for a protocol role.
keyExports.getModelHints: The model hints for an agent name.

assumptions: Model hints are keyed by client surface rather than by provider: a client can remain a projection target even when it is not available as a worker provider.
Tool lists are curated per role rather than derived, which is what makes a read-only role genuinely read-only.
The definitions are static data; nothing here reads configuration or the filesystem.
risks: The curated tool lists drift when a new MCP tool ships without being added, so a role silently lacks a capability.

Tool lists are curated per role rather than derived from the tool registry, and they are declarative metadata: the read-only roles carry the annotation-writing tools. Read-only capability is declared by canEditFiles, which the result validator enforces against reported file changes.
Because the manifests are projected into client files at onboarding, an edit here does not reach an already-onboarded workspace until setup runs again.
patterns: One definition list drives three consumers: the MCP manifest tool, the projection into client files, and the doctor's drift check.
invariants: A manifest name matches the identity of the client agent file it is projected into.
Every protocol role resolves to exactly one canonical manifest.
annotation.integrationPoints: Manifest and role types come from mod:repovine/src/agents/protocol; the definitions are served by the MCP manifest tool, rendered into client assets by the CLI onboarding path, and read by the projection renderers in mod:repovine/src/cli/agent-projection.
annotation.dataFlow: definition records -> manifest lookups for the MCP tool -> rendered agent files in the client trees -> read back by the doctor when checking for drift.

annotation.summary: Authoritative Zod schema module for Agent Protocol v1. Declares the assignment a harness hands an agent, the run result an agent returns, the compliance report repovine produces about that run, the agent manifests, the context-quality artifacts and context packs, and the capability result shapes for architecture audit and code review. Exports the protocol descriptor and the JSON Schema projection for harnesses that are not TypeScript.

keyExports.AGENT_JSON_SCHEMAS: JSON Schema projection of every public protocol schema, keyed by SCHEMA_IDS, for non-TypeScript harnesses.
keyExports.AGENT_ROLES: The role vocabulary the protocol recognizes: main, explorer, implementer, annotation-writer, architecture-auditor, code-reviewer.
keyExports.AgentAssignmentSchema: The task a harness assigns: run id, task, scope, acceptance criteria, requested checks, context session.
keyExports.AgentComplianceReportSchema: repovine's verdict: validity, errors, ungrounded and inconsistent annotations, required followups.
keyExports.AgentManifestSchema: The manifest describing a role's capabilities and obligations.
keyExports.AgentRunResultSchema: The public run artifact, including compliance flags and the optional context/audit/review payloads.
keyExports.ContextPackSchema: A context pack of resolved anchors handed to an agent.
keyExports.ContextSessionPolicySchema: Context-session policy: phase, enforcement mode, thresholds.
keyExports.PROJECTION_TARGETS: The client surfaces the protocol can be projected into: agents-md, cursor, codex, claude, json.
keyExports.REQUESTED_CHECKS: The checks an assignment may request (dependencies, config, runtime-flow, architecture, code-review, annotations, tests), which drive compliance flag validation.
keyExports.RUN_STATUSES: The terminal run statuses: complete, partial, blocked, failed.
keyExports.buildAgentProtocol: Returns the AgentProtocol descriptor: protocolVersion, schema ids, mcpTools (empty — CLI-only), and cliCommands.

assumptions: Sub-agent schemas (SubagentAssignment, SubagentHandoff) are internal: an external harness consumes the aggregated AgentRunResult rather than the per-sub-agent shapes.
Context-quality types (CONTEXT_PHASES, CONTEXT_ENFORCEMENT_MODES) are re-exported from src/context-quality/types.js, which stays their source of truth.
Requested checks are the mechanism by which an assignment decides which compliance flags are validated.
Agent Protocol is CLI-only for harness/integration (AGENT_PROTOCOL_MCP_TOOLS is an empty array); worker MCP exposes context tools only, not the protocol validators.

risks.text: Published protocol contract: the version literal, schema shapes and JSON Schema projection are what external harnesses and the managed AGENTS.md sections are built against, so a version bump or a field change lands outside this repo before it lands here.

risks: A requested check with no corresponding validation path silently passes, since compliance flags are driven by the requested set rather than by an exhaustive sweep.
patterns: The run result JSON block in the managed agent instructions is the harness contract itself, not illustrative prose.
Every protocol surface is a Zod schema first, with the TypeScript type inferred from it, so validation and typing cannot drift apart.
invariants: The compliance report (AgentComplianceReportSchema) is constructed by the validator and never parsed from agent-supplied input.
TypeScript types are inferred from the Zod schemas (z.infer), so the runtime validator and static types cannot drift apart.

ungroundedAnnotations and inconsistentAnnotations on the compliance report are mode-independent observable facts, not a verdict; only hard inconsistencies (keyExports/sideEffects) land there, advisory env mismatches stay in warnings.
annotation.integrationPoints: Served through the agent-protocol CLI commands (repovine agents protocol/manifests/validate-*/compliance), enforced by mod:repovine/src/agents/validation, projected into client surfaces by mod:repovine/src/cli/agent-projection, and re-exports context-quality shapes from mod:repovine/src/context-quality/types.
annotation.dataFlow: Zod schemas define AgentAssignment/AgentRunResult -> harness sends assignment, agent returns result -> compliance validator checks result against schema plus observable graph/annotation state -> AgentComplianceReport.

annotation.summary: Loads the repository's own role definitions from the roles section of the committed repovine config. It validates rather than transforms: each brief is served byte for byte including its frontmatter, and a brief carrying protocol markers or an embedded result block is reported as a structured error for the repository owner to fix rather than being cleaned up. A working-tree brief path is admitted by the shared containment guard, so a link resolving outside the repository is refused. Given a tree-ish it reads the config and every brief from that committed revision instead of the working tree.

keyExports.LoadRolesOptions: Options: an optional tree-ish to read the config and briefs from.
keyExports.ProjectRole: One role: id, optional description, ownership scope, brief path, verbatim brief bytes, their hash, and any non-blocking advisories.
keyExports.ProjectRoleSource: The load result: whether the config opted in at all, plus the roles.
keyExports.loadProjectRoleSource: Loads and validates the role definitions, returning the source or a list of errors.

assumptions: An absent roles section is a valid state meaning the repository has not opted in, not an error.
A role id must be lowercase kebab-case, and a brief path must stay inside the repository after symlink resolution.
A brief path that names a file which does not exist is reported as unreadable rather than as an escape.
The scope defaults to the repository root when a role does not declare one.
The hash is taken over the exact brief bytes, so any edit to the file changes it, including whitespace.

sideEffects.description: reads the config and the brief files from the working tree
reads the config and briefs from a committed revision through git when a tree-ish is given

risks.text: The roles section of the committed repovine config is a contract repository owners author against, and the brief bytes are served verbatim to agents; changing the accepted shape or the id rules invalidates configurations that live outside this repository.

risks: Contamination detection matches a fixed set of literal markers, so a brief carrying protocol content in some other form passes validation and reaches an agent unchanged.
A scope path excluded from the scan configuration is reported only as a non-blocking advisory, so a role can be loaded successfully while owning paths the graph never indexes.
patterns: Validate and refuse rather than sanitize: preparing the file is the repository owner's job, which keeps the served bytes predictable.
The dependency direction is strictly one way, from consumer through the CLI into this loader, so no harness or client concepts appear in these types.
invariants: A brief is served byte for byte, frontmatter included; nothing is stripped or rewritten.
The hash is over the exact bytes served, so a consumer can pin the prose it received.
A tree-ish read takes both the config and every brief from that same revision.
annotation.integrationPoints: Reads the roles section of the committed repovine config; containment guard from mod:repovine/src/fs/containment; exposed read-only through the agents roles CLI command and consumed in-process when the role catalog is assembled.
annotation.dataFlow: config roles section -> per-role validation of id, scope and brief path -> verbatim brief read plus hash -> role source, or a list of structured errors.

annotation.summary: Schema validation and Agent Protocol compliance checking. It compares result claims with the graph, annotation state, manifests, and recorded context sessions. Evidence-backed protocol and annotation findings can still fail harness compliance; the context-quality score is recomputed and reported with warnings/followups but remains advisory after D5 falsified the weighted score.

keyExports.CheckComplianceInput: The result and its assignment, the state, the manifest, and whether the run began greenfield.
keyExports.ComplianceState: What the check needs: the repository, graph, snapshot, annotations, and the context-quality accessors.
keyExports.SchemaValidation: A parse outcome with its errors, warnings and any unsupported version.
keyExports.checkCompliance: The compliance pass: grounding, scope, annotation state, quality and context session, producing the report.
keyExports.nodeInAnnotationScope: Whether a node falls inside the assignment's scope hints.
keyExports.resolveGraphNodeId: Resolves a caller-supplied identifier to one the graph holds.
keyExports.validateAndCheckCompliance: Schema validation followed by compliance in one call.
keyExports.validateAssignment: Parses an assignment against its schema.
keyExports.validateReviewInput: Parses a review input and cross-checks its declared changes against the result.
keyExports.validateRunResult: Parses a run result against its schema.

assumptions: Enforcement mode decides severity for evidence-backed annotation and protocol findings; context-quality verdicts remain advisory in both modes until the labelled-corpus return bar is met.
The declared phase constrains what a result may claim, and a scoped sub-agent is judged against its own scope.
Aggregate roll-ups that are merely unannotated stay advisory because they are derived rather than authored.
Environment inconsistencies stay advisory because dynamic access is under-captured.

sideEffects.description: a valid report consumes the run's context session unless retention is requested

risks: The provenance gate exists because the quality score measures completeness rather than correctness: without it an agent can write plausible notes and score well.
The greenfield exemption depends on the caller: the run's own writes are known here, but a sibling sub-agent's writes land in the same shared file.

An omitted assignment does not skip compliance, it disarms the assignment-derived gates: runId linkage, phase and scope judgements, and the context-session requirement all go inert, while manifest fields, declared graph nodes, declared annotations and provenance still run and still hard-fail. Weak tool usage is still scored whenever the result carries a contextSessionId, but nothing can make it enforceable without an assignment, so it only ever surfaces as a warning.
Scope membership is decided from the supplied hints, so an assignment whose scope omits a form the nodes actually carry judges the wrong set.
patterns: Evidence-backed graph, protocol, annotation consistency, and provenance checks remain enforceable; the unvalidated context score is one explicit advisory exception.
A rejected advisory context report is retained for review, while accepted reports are consumed after the remaining compliance checks pass.
Pre-existing annotations are never re-judged because only writes claimed by the current run are in scope.
invariants: Context-quality acceptHandoff=false alone never makes compliance invalid until the validation return bar is met.
Rejected context reports remain available instead of being consumed as successful handoffs.
Provenance applies to code modules only; derived roll-ups are excluded.
Identifiers in a result must resolve against the graph.
An annotate-phase result never reports source edits.
annotation.integrationPoints: Schemas and the protocol version come from mod:repovine/src/agents/protocol and the role manifests from mod:repovine/src/agents/manifests; annotation state, quality and staleness from mod:repovine/src/annotations/store and mod:repovine/src/annotations/maintenance; effect vocabulary from mod:repovine/src/annotations/side-effect-vocab; module classification from mod:repovine/src/annotations/module-kind; ownership resolution from mod:repovine/src/graph/node-ids; the context-quality shapes from mod:repovine/src/context-quality/types. Exposed through the validation and compliance commands of the command line.
annotation.dataFlow: result and assignment -> schema parse -> evidence-backed phase/scope/annotation/provenance checks -> recomputed advisory context report -> errors only from validated evidence gates, plus warnings and required followups -> accepted session consumption.

annotation.summary: The entry points for architecture analysis: run the detector suite over a scope and return a balanced page of findings, or expand one finding into detail. It takes a small state slice rather than the server runtime, so the analysis can be exercised without the server around it.

keyExports.RefactoringOpportunityDetailArgs: The finding identifier plus the scope and node cap for its expansion.
keyExports.RefactoringReportArgs: Scope, categories, minimum confidence, page limit, and the two behaviour toggles.
keyExports.RefactoringState: What the analysis needs: the graph, the module index, annotations, and optionally the snapshot, thresholds, propagation settings and entrypoints.
keyExports.refactoringCategoriesFromFindingId: Resolves a finding identifier back to the categories that must be rerun to produce it.
keyExports.runRefactoringOpportunityDetail: Expands one finding by identifier, with its affected nodes and the edges between them.
keyExports.runRefactoringReport: Runs the detectors for a scope and returns a capped, category-balanced page of findings.

assumptions: An empty detector registry raises with an explanation rather than returning no findings, because registration happens through a side-effect import and a caller that reached the analysis without it would otherwise see a clean report on an unanalyzed repository.

A detector is skipped when none of its categories were asked for, and again when it declares an applicability test that no in-scope module satisfies — safe because such a detector emits nothing anyway. A later per-category filter then drops categories a multi-category detector produced but the caller did not request.
The detail path searches the full uncapped list and with no confidence floor, so a valid identifier resolves even when the finding sits past the report's page or below its threshold.

A finding identifier maps to its categories by prefix, and failing that by the longest matching detector identifier from the registry, so a new detector's prefix round-trips without a table to update.
Findings are deduplicated per category and primary node before any cap, so the page reflects distinct problems rather than repeated views of one.
Everything here is a read over the state; nothing is written.
Verified 2026-07-23: runRefactoringReport/runRefactoringOpportunityDetail signatures and detector-bootstrap/detector-registry imports unchanged; content-hash refresh only.
risks: The page is balanced across categories rather than strictly ranked, so the highest-confidence findings overall are not necessarily the ones returned — a caller reading the page as a priority order will misread it.
The confidence floor defaults to a middle value, so a report with no arguments silently omits everything below it; the number is reported back but the omission is not.
Detector applicability is cached per predicate for the run, so a detector whose applicability depends on anything beyond the module shape would be evaluated once and reused.
patterns: Registry dispatch with two cheap gates before running anything, so an unrequested or inapplicable detector costs nothing.
One collection path serving both modes, with the report capping what the detail path deliberately does not.
invariants: A cold registry fails loudly rather than reporting zero findings.
The detail path never misses a finding the report could have shown.
Requested categories bound what is returned, whatever a detector produced.
annotation.integrationPoints: Wrapped by the analysis tool under mod:repovine/src/mcp/tools; detectors are registered by mod:repovine/src/analysis/architecture/detector-bootstrap and resolved through mod:repovine/src/analysis/architecture/detector-registry; thresholds from mod:repovine/src/analysis/architecture/config; scope resolution, sorting and expansion from the scope, finding and detail modules beside it; annotation state from mod:repovine/src/annotations/store and staleness from mod:repovine/src/annotations/propagation.

annotation.summary: The tunable thresholds that decide whether an architecture detector emits a finding. Settings arrive in three tiers: per call through the tool arguments, per repository through the configuration file which is what this module models, and a hardcoded research tier covering the confidence formulas, the severity mapping and the truncation budgets, which is not exposed. A named strictness profile supplies the baseline and individual knobs may be overridden on top of it.

keyExports.AnnotationRiskQualityByKind: The minimum annotation quality expected of each module kind.
keyExports.DEFAULT_THRESHOLDS: The middle profile, exposed so other layers can name the default.
keyExports.RefactoringFileConfig: What a repository may set: a profile, per-knob overrides, or both.
keyExports.RefactoringThresholds: Every threshold group, one per detector family, including the security-sensitive ones.
keyExports.resolveThresholds: Merges the chosen profile with the per-knob overrides into a complete threshold set.

assumptions: The middle profile is the calibration target; the other two are relative perturbations chosen to keep a report readable rather than independently tuned.
For most groups the direction is plain: a looser profile lowers the bar to emit and produces more findings, a stricter one raises it and produces fewer.
The per-kind annotation quality bars deep-merge rather than replace, so tightening one kind leaves the calibrated defaults for the others in place.
The derived-stale penalty does not decide whether a module is surfaced — the detector always surfaces it — it raises the bar that decides how confidently the finding is stated.
A repository that sets nothing gets the middle profile.

risks.text: Within the annotation group the direction is mixed: the per-kind quality bars, the derived-stale penalty and the stale hop limit all tighten under a stricter profile and surface more modules, while the importance floor that decides candidacy rises with it and removes modules before quality is computed at all. A caller changing strictness gets a different population of annotation findings rather than simply more or fewer, and must read those findings themselves instead of inferring a direction.

risks: The scalar quality threshold and the per-kind bars move in opposite directions across profiles, and the scalar applies only when no per-kind bar exists — so it matters solely for a custom configuration that omits them, where its direction is the reverse of what the profile name suggests.

Lowering an evidence threshold on a security group raises the false-positive rate without changing what is detected, so a report can become noisy in a way that reads as a code problem rather than a configuration one.
Nothing reports the effective thresholds, so a repository running under a profile it did not intend produces findings that look like the code changed.
patterns: Complete profiles rather than deltas: each named profile carries every threshold, so reading one shows the whole posture without composing.
Configuration covers what a repository legitimately tunes; the formulas that decide confidence and severity stay out of reach on purpose.
invariants: Resolution is profile first, then per-knob overrides.
An absent configuration resolves to the middle profile.
Overriding one kind's quality bar never clears the others.
extensionPoints: A new detector family adds its threshold group to the interface and a value to all three profiles.
A new security detector follows the same evidence-score or signal-count shape as the existing ones.
annotation.integrationPoints: The module kinds the per-kind bars are keyed by come from mod:repovine/src/annotations/module-kind; the resolved thresholds are consumed by every detector in the architecture analysis. Strictness reaches the analysis only through the repository configuration file — resolved once when configuration is loaded, named by no tool argument, so a change takes effect only after a configuration reload.
annotation.dataFlow: repository configuration → named profile as the baseline → per-knob overrides merged on top, with the per-kind quality bars deep-merged → a complete threshold set handed to every detector.

annotation.summary: Legacy analyze_architecture detector implementations over RepositoryGraph, ModuleInfo semantic hints, and AnnotationStore; emits RefactoringFinding[] per category (duplicateLike, boundary, godModule, serverHandlerOrchestration, domainShape, clientBusinessLogic, flowConvergence, effectSpaghetti, propDrillingOrchestration, uiDomainCoupling). annotation.summary: Local recovery snapshots named annotations.backup.<timestamp>.json, newest MAX_ANNOTATION_BACKUPS retained per directory. AnnotationStore writes failed-load and shrink-guard snapshots beside the annotations file; mergeAnnotationsOnDisk writes conflict snapshots into .repovine/annotation-backups (covered by the managed .gitignore block) via the dir option. Content matching a retained backup reuses that file and returns its path, so a caller disclosing 'your bytes are recoverable here' keeps the disclosure when deduplication kicks in.

keyExports.MAX_ANNOTATION_BACKUPS: Retention count; older backups are rotated away after each write.
keyExports.writeAnnotationBackup: Snapshot bytes into dir (default: the annotations file's directory); returns written(path) | duplicate(path) | failed(error).

assumptions: Backups are local recovery files, never read back automatically. Those written into .repovine/annotation-backups are git-ignored; those written beside the annotations file are untracked and surface in git status.
Dedup compares size first, then bytes, over retained backups in the same directory.

sideEffects.description: Lists and reads annotations.backup.*.json for dedup
Creates the target dir, atomically writes a backup, unlinks rotated-out ones

risks.text: The writer never throws; a caller that is about to destroy the snapshotted bytes must check for status 'failed' and abort instead of proceeding.

invariants: A caller never fails because a backup failed; the status is returned, not thrown.
At most MAX_ANNOTATION_BACKUPS backups survive a write in one directory.
written and duplicate both name a path holding exactly the requested bytes.
annotation.integrationPoints: mod:repovine/src/annotations/store createBackup; mod:repovine/src/annotations/maintenance mergeAnnotationsOnDisk (dir: .repovine/annotation-backups); mod:repovine/src/fs/atomic writeFileAtomicSync.
annotation.dataFlow: caller bytes -> dedup scan of retained backups in dir -> atomic write of annotations.backup.<ts>.json -> rotation to MAX_ANNOTATION_BACKUPS

annotation.summary: Detects the two ways a carrier link can be broken.
